# Breeding systems are correlated with environmental factors

- Factors like the strength and bias in parental care and distribution of resources interact to shape breeding systems

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/systems.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [Katherine Furniss](https://open.lib.umn.edu/evosex/chapter/10-7-correlation-of-environmental-factors-with-mating-systems/)  

# Monogamy

- 2 parents involved in raising & caring for offspring
- ~90% of species
- Duration: 1 nesting attempt to 1 breeding season to a lifetime
- **Extra pair copulations common** (~11% of offspring; consistent with "social monogamy")

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/trumpeter2.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Cygnus buccinator*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/55977761)  

# Consequences of extra pair copulation  

- Male Barn Swallows protect females from competitors during her most fertile period, but pursue extrapair copulations after it has ended

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/swallow_chasing.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Beecher & Beecher 1979)    

# Polygamy

- Any mating system involving multiple mates of the opposite sex
- ~3% of species 
- Strong variation in reproductive success for one species -> strong sexual selection
- Can be **polygyny**,  **polyandry**, or **polygynandry**

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.55\linewidth]{images/wilson.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Phalaropus tricolor*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/60920031)

# Polygyny

- **Territorial polygyny**: multiple females join a single male territory with high quality resources
- Associated with clumped resource distributions
- Found in ~2% of spp. overall
- Found in 14/278 breeding North American songbirds, 11 of which nest in marshes or grasslands

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/rwbb.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c0Lw23yQFwQ

\hfill \tiny [*Agelaius phoeniceus*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/49503081)

# Polygyny

- **Lek polygyny**: multiple females mate with a limited number of males from communal lek or solitary arena
- Females do all parental care

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/sagegr.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c0Lw23yQFwQ  
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cLnbiTkj1TQ

\hfill \tiny [*Centrocercus urophasianus*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/46364181)

# Polyandry

- Multiple males mate with a single female 
- <1% of species; most common in Charadriiformes (due to fixed, 4-egg clutch?)
- Sexual selection on females can lead to sex-role reversal

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/spsp.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Actitis macularius*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/35730281)

# What mating system is likely to evolve under dispersed resources? 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.55\linewidth]{images/ammo.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*Ammospiza caudacuta*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/60716171))

\normalsize

a) polyandry
b) polygamy
c) promiscuity
d) monogamy


# Testosterone and sex role reversal in Spotted Sandpipers

- Females have higher testosterone, fight each other for males
- Males incubate eggs, defend territories, provide most parental care

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/endocrine.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Sexual selection in Wattled Jacanas

- Females have more mates, greater variance in reproductive success
- Females with larger tarsi have greater mating success

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/jacana2.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([ML27855351](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/27855351); Emlen & Wrege 2004)  

# Polygynandry 

- Both males and females have >1 mate
- <1% of species: tinamous, ratites, some parrots
- Males incubate mixed clutches of >1 female

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/emu.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Dromaius novaehollandiae*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/460698641) 

# Polygynandry in Electus Parrots

- Females depend on males for almost all food, stay in nest trees
- Telemetry data shows male territories overlap with each other and female trees
- Males equally likely to have offspring with females across territory (and vice versa)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.55\linewidth]{images/ec_poly.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([*ML81458761s*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/81458761); Heinsohn et al. 2024)   

# Evolution of social mating systems

- "Divorce" in monogamous birds associated with male promiscuity and migration distance

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/divorce.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Chen et al. Douvas 2023)    

# Evolution of mating systems

- Monogamy is ubiquitous, ancestral for most species
- Reversion from lekking to monogamy is hard
- Reversion from resource-defense polygamy is a little easier

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/mating_systems.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Marcondes & Douvas 2024)    

# Brood Parasitism

- Female of one species lays an egg in the nest of another species
- Boosts reproductive success without additional parental care
- Can be **intraspecific** or **interspecific**, **obligate** or **non-obligate**, **specialized** on a host species or **generalist**

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/cowbird.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Molothrus ater*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/84247171) 

# *Vidua* Brood Parasites

- *Vidua* species mimic grassfinch hosts through gape patterns and sounds of host nestlings

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/vidua.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Jamie et al. 2020)

# What kind of brood parasites are *Vidua*? 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/vidua.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Jamie et al. 2020)

\normalsize 

a) generalist, non-obligate, intraspecific
b) specialized, obligate, interspecific
c) generalist, obligate, intraspecific
b) specialized, non-obligate, intraspecific

# Cospeciation in *Vidua* and hosts?

- **Cospeciation** is simultaneous divergence in interacting lineages (host / parasites)
- $H$: Shared divergence times in hosts and parasites 
- Limited evidence, but strong correlation from "clade-limited colonization"

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/cospeciation.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Sorenson et al. 2004)


# Cooperative Breeding 

- "Helpers" care for young that are not theirs
- <9% of birds
- Driven by **kin selection** (ensure success of genes shared in distant relatives), **reciprocal altruism** (you scratch my back I'll scratch yours), ecological constraints, practice...

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/scrub_jay.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Aphelocoma coerulescens*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/230141521) 

# Hormonal differences between breeders and helpers

- Male helpers have lower testosterone than breeders
- Female helpers have estradiol peak when breeder is incubating and they disperse to find their own territory 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/cooperate.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Schoech 1998) 

# Evidence for kin selection in White-fronted Bee-eaters

- "Helpers" preferentially assist most closely related mating pairs, maximizing their "inclusive" reproductive fitness

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/beeeater.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Emlen et al. 1995)
